summary: Captures requirements for improved archiving of IETF email lists and for web-based browsing and searching. Participants wanted better search and the existing archive mechanism could be more efficient. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: People keep old letters in a big box and want to find them quickly. This memo lists what a better box and search should do.

subtitle: What the IETF wanted from a better system for archiving, browsing and searching its mailing lists.

tldr.problem: IETF participants rely on mailing lists but found cross-list and long-range searches of the archives slow and error prone, and the archive mechanism kept duplicate stores.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists requirements for web search and browsing, archiving active lists, import and export, redundancy, administration and keeping old links working.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document only. It does not specify a design, and it notes that building the tool does not affect Internet security in any significant fashion.

today: RFC 6778 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It records requirements, not a specific implementation.

sections.title: Why Better Archives
sections.content:
The IETF does its work largely over email lists. Document editors, shepherds, chairs and area directors may need to review all discussion of a draft, spread across a working group list, directorate lists and the IETF general list. Existing tools need several manually coordinated steps that are error prone, and without a local copy most lists need brute force searching.

The current archive practice also keeps duplicate stores for the web and ftp interfaces, which hurts storage and replication and risks inconsistency. This memo captures requirements for improved archiving and searching.
sections.plainLanguage: Finding an old letter means digging through several boxes by hand, and some letters are stored twice. A better system would fix both.

sections.title: Search, Browse and Access
sections.content:
The system must offer a web interface to search and browse archived messages, by thread or by date, across any subset of lists. Threading should consider both Message-Id/References/In-Reply-To and matching subject lines. Searches must combine, with AND, OR and NOT, the sender, a date range, the subject, the body and message headers such as an exact Message-Id.

Each message must have a long-term stable URI suitable for citing in email, ideally also given in an Archived-At header field (RFC 5064). Searches should also be shareable by URI, and results may differ when re-run. Credentials, when needed, must use the datatracker's authentication. Open archives must not require credentials, restricted archives must be limitable by login, and their messages must be distinguishable in results.
sections.plainLanguage: You should be able to look through all the boxes at once, with any clue like who wrote it or when. Every letter should have a permanent address you can share, and private letters are only for people with a key.

sections.title: Archiving, Import and Export
sections.content:
The archive system must accept messages from various list manager packages. IETF lists use Mailman, and for lists at other organizations it must accept messages by subscribing to the external list. When lists move to IETF servers, the system must import their archives, at a minimum in mbox format (RFC 4155), and should import Maildir-style archives. A separate lossless converter is acceptable.

Users and administrators must be able to export messages in mbox format, export a whole list, and export messages in a date range. Export in Maildir and of search results should be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The box must accept letters from other boxes and let people take copies out, in common formats.

sections.title: Redundancy, Administration and Transition
sections.content:
The systems must make it possible to serve archive, search and browse from geographically distributed servers. They must support one active and one standby server, which is the current configuration, and should support multiple standbys and multiple active servers for search and browse. Replication traffic should be on the order of the size of new or changed messages, whether via database replication or filesystem copying such as rsync.

Administrators must be able to add and remove archived lists and add or delete messages, and the system should log such actions. Existing links into the old MHonArc archive must keep working, but should reach the message as archived in the new system.
sections.plainLanguage: There should be a spare copy ready if the main one breaks, and the librarian should be able to add or remove things. Old bookmarks must still lead to the right letter.

sections.title: Other Considerations and Security
sections.content:
The archive and search functions should anticipate internationalized email addresses (RFC 6531, RFC 6532), though there is no firm requirement. The system must also anticipate integrating with a system that provides IMAP access.

The RFC says a new search and archive tool does not affect Internet security in any significant fashion. It warns that searching can be I/O and CPU intensive, so implementors should consider maliciously crafted searches and denial-of-service attempts, and should authenticate administrative access and configure message paths to avoid unauthorized insertion.
sections.plainLanguage: Watch out for people who ask the librarian huge questions to wear them out, and make sure only the right people can put letters in the box.
